title: Three perfect days in New York: Halloween, then the marathon
dek: A Friday of museums and Grand Central, a Saturday that ends on Sixth Avenue for the Village Halloween Parade, and a Sunday in Brooklyn cheering the marathon, with an extra hour to spare.

hero.caption: The Brooklyn Bridge, the start of a Manhattan skyline that is at its sharpest in late-autumn light.

intro:
New York packs two of its biggest street parties into this one weekend. On Saturday, October 31, the **Village Halloween Parade** marches up Sixth Avenue at 7 p.m. under this year's theme, *Body & Soul*, with Joey Arias as grand marshal; anyone in costume can join in. Less than a day later, on Sunday, November 1, about 60,000 runners set off from Staten Island for the **TCS New York City Marathon**, which this year marks the 50th anniversary of its five-borough route and has its first course change in 15 years, in the Bronx.

Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. that same Sunday, so you get an extra hour after the parade. You will want it.

The plan below works around both. Friday stays uptown and in Midtown, with the Met's *Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous*, a walk through Central Park before the finish-line bleachers fill it, and oysters under the Guastavino vaults at Grand Central. Saturday is downtown: the Whitney's two Roy Lichtenstein shows, the High Line, the Strand, an early pie on Bleecker Street, then the parade and a late set from Robert Glasper's Robtober residency at the Blue Note. Sunday crosses to Brooklyn to watch the runners on Lafayette Avenue, then the Brooklyn Museum's new *Art of Manga* and dinner in Prospect Heights.

Late October here usually means cool mornings and the trees in Central Park and Prospect Park on the turn. Bring layers and a costume, even a modest one; on Halloween night, the people without one are the ones who stand out.

days.title: Friday: the Upper East Side to Grand Central
days.intro: Art in the morning, the park in the afternoon, and an evening inside the most handsome train station in America. The Met stays open until 9 p.m. on Fridays if you would rather linger.

stops.name: Café Sabarsky
stops.text: Start the weekend in Vienna. The café on the ground floor of the Neue Galerie, a Beaux-Arts mansion across from Central Park, serves Viennese-inspired food under chef Christopher Engel; have a Viennese coffee and something from the cake case, which is reason enough to eat dessert at 9 a.m. The museum's galleries are closed until November 12 for its 25th-anniversary exhibition, but the café and the design shop are open. Breakfast and lunch are first come, first served, so arrive at opening.

stops.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
stops.text: Ten blocks north is the reason to come this autumn: **Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous**, on view through January 31, which treats Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock as peers rather than as a famous painter and his wife, following them from 1940s New York to Long Island and Krasner's work after Pollock's death in 1956. Then pick one more: *Costume Art* or the Louis C. Tiffany drawings in *Designing the Gilded Age*. Adult tickets are $30; New York State residents pay what they wish. Buying online lets you use any entrance.

stops.name: Lexington Candy Shop
stops.text: A luncheonette that has been pouring malteds on this corner for about a century, with a counter, stools and a soda fountain that nobody has tried to modernize. Order a grilled cheese or a burger and an egg cream or a malted, and sit at the counter if you can. Its photogenic interior has made it famous online, and the neighborhood site Upper East Site reported lines down the block this summer; a weekday mid-afternoon is your best chance.

stops.name: Central Park: Bethesda Terrace and the Mall
stops.text: Enter at Fifth Avenue and 79th Street and drift south past the Ramble to **Bethesda Terrace**, where the arcade's tiled ceiling and the Angel of the Waters fountain look best in low autumn sun. Continue down the elm-lined Mall and leave at 59th Street. On the west side you will see the marathon's finish area near Tavern on the Green taking shape; the park gets very crowded by Sunday, so today is the day to see it calm. Allow an hour and a half at an easy pace.

stops.name: Winter Village at Bryant Park
stops.text: The Bank of America Winter Village opened on October 28 for its new season, so you get the rink and the holiday shops before the December crowds. Admission to the ice is free if you bring skates; rentals start at about $19. Skate as the office towers light up, browse the shop stalls (open until 8 p.m.), or take a hot drink at The Lodge, the bar and food hall beside the rink, open until 10 p.m. Grand Central is a five-minute walk east along 42nd Street.

stops.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
stops.text: Down the ramps from the main concourse, under vaulted tile ceilings, this is the place to eat oysters in New York on a Friday night. Order a rotating dozen from both coasts, the oyster pan roast, and a martini; diners recommend the lobster roll. Before you go in, stand in the Whispering Gallery outside the entrance and speak into a corner. The dining room is open Monday to Friday only, so Friday is your one chance this weekend; the last seating is 9:30 p.m.

stops.name: The Campbell
stops.addr: Grand Central Terminal, off 43rd St and Vanderbilt Ave
stops.text: Finish upstairs in the 1920s office of the financier John W. Campbell, a room of leaded-glass windows, a stone fireplace and his old steel safe, reopened as a bar in 2017. Sit in the main room if there is live jazz, or out in the Palm Court overlooking the terminal. Cocktails generally run $20 and up, so make it one good one before the train or the subway back.

days.title: Saturday: downtown on Halloween
days.intro: Art and a long walk by day, then the Village at its most theatrical. Plan to be on the east side of Sixth Avenue by about 6:30 p.m.; crossing it during the parade is very difficult.

stops.name: Buvette
stops.text: Jody Williams's tiny French bar à vin on a tree-lined Village street opens at 8 a.m. daily and is at its best in the morning: fresh croissants, a croque madame, coffee at the marble counter, and the room to yourself before brunch arrives. It does not take reservations, which is another reason to go early. Grove Street, one of the prettiest blocks in the city, is worth a slow look on the way out.

stops.name: Whitney Museum of American Art
stops.text: Renzo Piano's museum at the foot of the High Line has two Roy Lichtenstein shows on, *Roy Lichtenstein: Like New* among them, plus *The Lost World: The Art of Minnie Evans* and Charles Burchfield's watercolors in *Elemental*. Save time for the outdoor terraces on the upper floors, which look straight down the Hudson. Open 10:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturdays; adults pay $30 and visitors 25 and under get in free. Book a timed ticket online.

stops.name: The High Line to Chelsea Market
stops.text: Climb to the High Line at Gansevoort Street, right outside the Whitney, and walk north on the old elevated freight line, its plantings gone copper and gold, as far as 16th Street (it is open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. through November). Drop down into Chelsea Market, the old Nabisco factory, for lunch. Here the original Los Tacos No. 1 stand has been serving Tijuana-style tacos since 2013 and still draws a line at lunchtime. Order the adobada with everything and eat standing up, which is the only option. Then wander the market; Fishs Eddy opened a shop here in May, and Miznon's pitas are a good second lunch.

stops.name: Strand Book Store
stops.text: Walk east along 14th Street to the last survivor of Fourth Avenue's old Book Row, founded in 1927 and still family-owned. Four floors and some 2.5 million new, used and rare books; start at the discount racks outside, go up to the rare-book room, and come away with something you did not know you wanted. It's a good place to wait out a shower, too.

stops.name: John's of Bleecker Street
stops.text: A coal-fired pizzeria open since 1929, with wooden booths carved with decades of initials and whole pies only, no slices. It is mostly walk-in, which is exactly what you want on Halloween, and it sits a block west of the parade route. Order a plain pie or one with sausage and mushrooms. Eat early: once the parade starts, Sixth Avenue becomes a wall, so finish by 6:30 and cross to the east side while you still can.

stops.name: Village Halloween Parade
stops.addr: Sixth Ave, from Spring St to 16th St
stops.text: The 53rd parade steps off at 7 p.m., with the new puppet piece *Firehorse* in front and tens of thousands of costumed New Yorkers behind it, marching north on Sixth Avenue for two or three hours. The stretch from Bleecker Street up to 14th Street is the busiest; the southern end nearer SoHo is calmer. Watch from the east side so you can head to the Blue Note afterward, and fix a meeting point a few blocks off the avenue. To march, simply turn up in costume at the Canal Street staging area between 6:30 and 9 p.m.

stops.name: Blue Note
stops.text: The club, open since 1981 just off Sixth Avenue, is in the last days of Robert Glasper's eighth Robtober residency, and tonight is his Halloween show with bassist Derrick Hodge and drummer Chris Dave, a trio that slides from jazz into hip-hop and R&B. Seats go fast on Halloween, so book ahead and check set times on the ticket page. If it is sold out, Sunday's finale with the same band is the backup.

days.title: Sunday: Brooklyn on marathon day
days.intro: Clocks fall back at 2 a.m., so the morning comes an hour easier. Take the 2 or 3 train to Eastern Parkway and stay on this side of the course; driving anywhere near it today is a mistake.

stops.name: Cafe Mado
stops.text: A neighborhood café a block from the Brooklyn Museum, run by the team behind the former Oxalis and recommended by the Michelin Guide. Mornings bring coffee and a very good sausage, egg and cheese; at lunch, the Tony, a mortadella sandwich on a sesame bun, is the order. It opens at 8:30, and lunch and dinner tables can be booked on Resy.

stops.name: TCS New York City Marathon on Lafayette Avenue
stops.text: Walk north up Washington Avenue for about 20 minutes to Lafayette Avenue, where the course runs east through Fort Greene and Clinton Hill on its way to Bedford Avenue. The brownstone stoops here fill with neighbors, brass bands and homemade signs, and it is close enough to the start that the runners still look fresh. The professional fields pass first, then hours of everyone else; race waves leave Staten Island from about 8 to 11:30 a.m. Stay on the south side of the avenue so you can walk back without crossing the course.

stops.name: Brooklyn Museum
stops.text: Back down Washington Avenue, the museum opened its biggest autumn in years in early October. **Art of Manga** fills the Great Hall with hundreds of hand-drawn pages of Japanese comics, paired with *Manga Before Manga* from the museum's own Japanese collection; upstairs, *Cézanne to Modigliani* shows the Pearlman Collection's gift of modern art. Judy Chicago's *The Dinner Party* is always worth the climb. Open 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sundays; general admission is a suggested $16, ticketed shows $25. Closed Monday and Tuesday.

stops.name: Prospect Park
stops.text: From the museum, walk to Grand Army Plaza and into the park that Olmsted and Vaux, who designed Central Park, considered their better work. Follow the path onto the Long Meadow, nearly a mile of open lawn ringed by trees in full autumn color, and loop back past the Picnic House. It is quieter than Central Park on any day, and on marathon Sunday it is the calm half of the city. Allow an hour or two, and bring a coffee.

stops.name: Leland Eating & Drinking House
stops.text: A corner restaurant opened in 2020 by Randi Lee and Delfin Jaranilla, cooking what they call New York Mediterranean food from ingredients grown within about 100 miles. The kitchen bakes its bread daily and butchers whole fish; order the trout rillettes, the charred lemon mussels and the whole fried fish to share. The bar keeps around 40 vermouths, which makes a good toast to a long weekend. Book a table on Resy.

stay.name: The Carlyle, A Rosewood Hotel
stay.text: The Upper East Side's grand old hotel, open since 1930, is a short walk from the Met and Café Sabarsky, which makes Friday effortless. Have a nightcap under Ludwig Bemelmans's murals in Bemelmans Bar, or catch the cabaret at Café Carlyle. On Sunday the marathon passes up First Avenue and down Fifth to the east and west of you, so leave the car and take the subway to Brooklyn.

stay.name: Washington Square Hotel
stay.text: A hotel since 1902, with Art Deco touches, right on Washington Square Park and a few blocks east of the parade route and the Blue Note. On Halloween night you can walk home instead of fighting for a cab. Its restaurant, North Square, is closed for renovation, so plan on eating out, which in this neighborhood is no hardship.

stay.name: Arlo SoHo
stay.text: Compact, well-designed rooms near the Canal Street and Spring Street stations, with river views from the upper floors and a rooftop bar. It is close to the parade's southern end and an easy walk to the Whitney on Saturday. Rooms are small, so pack light, and book soon: rates climb sharply on a weekend like this.

events.name: Village Halloween Parade
events.where: Sixth Avenue, Spring St to 16th St, Greenwich Village
events.text: The 53rd annual parade, themed *Body & Soul*, with Joey Arias as grand marshal and the new puppet performance *Firehorse*. Free to watch; anyone in costume can march. NY1 broadcasts it live from 8 p.m.

events.name: TCS New York City Marathon
events.where: Staten Island to Central Park, through all five boroughs
events.text: About 60,000 runners on the 50th anniversary of the five-borough route, with a revised Bronx section. Cheer anywhere along the course; the finish is in Central Park near Tavern on the Green.

events.name: Harry Styles: Together, Together. Harryween.
events.text: The last two nights of Harry Styles's 30-show Garden residency, which began August 26, are his Halloween shows. Expect costumes in the crowd and resale prices to match.

events.name: Robtober at the Blue Note
events.text: Robert Glasper closes his month-long residency with Derrick Hodge and Chris Dave: Friday (with Isaiah Sharkey), a Halloween show on Saturday and the finale on Sunday.

events.name: Rangers vs. Edmonton Oilers
events.text: Connor McDavid's Oilers visit the Garden on marathon night. A good way to end the weekend if you would rather shout than sit down to dinner.

know: **From the airports.** From JFK, take the AirTrain ($8.75) to Jamaica and the E train or the LIRR into Manhattan; the E is about 35 to 40 minutes from Jamaica to Midtown. Taxis from JFK to Manhattan charge a flat $70 plus tolls, surcharges and tip. From Newark, the AirTrain connects to NJ Transit trains to Penn Station. From LaGuardia, take a taxi or the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus to the Jackson Heights subway hub.

**Clocks go back.** Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 1; clocks fall back to 1 a.m. Your phone will adjust, but check any hotel alarm clock, and remember sunset arrives an hour earlier on Sunday.

**Marathon closures.** On Sunday, closures begin around 7 a.m. and affect the Verrazzano-Narrows, Pulaski, Queensboro, Willis Avenue and Madison Avenue bridges, Fourth, Lafayette and Bedford Avenues in Brooklyn, First and Fifth Avenues and Central Park South in Manhattan, and parts of Queens and the Bronx. Use the subway, give yourself extra time, and do not plan a Sunday morning taxi to the airport across the course.
**Halloween night.** Sixth Avenue below 16th Street is closed to traffic for the parade, and the nearby subway stations are packed. Pick a meeting point a few blocks off the route and expect to walk.

**Paying for transit.** Tap a contactless card or phone at any subway turnstile or bus reader with OMNY; a ride costs $3. Use the same card each time, because OMNY caps your fares after 12 paid rides in seven days.
**Tipping.** In restaurants, 18 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill is normal; at bars, a dollar or two a drink; for taxis, 15 to 20 percent.
